source_text: Οὗτος οὖν μόνος καὶ κατὰ πάντων θεὸς λόγον πρῶτον ἐννοηθεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ, οὐ λόγον ὡς φωνήν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐνδιάθετον τοῦ παντὸς λογισμόν. Τοῦτον μόνον ἐξ ὄντων ἐγέννα· τὸ γὰρ ὂν αὐτὸς ὁ πατὴρ ἦν, ἐξ οὗ τὸ γεννηθέν. Αἴτιον τοῖς γινομένοις λόγος ἦν, ἐν ἑαυτῷ φέρων τὸ θέλειν τοῦ γεγεννηκότος, οὐκ ἄπειρος τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ἐννοίας· ἅμα γὰρ τῷ ἐκ τοῦ γεννήσαντος προελθεῖν, πρωτότοκος τούτου γενόμενος φωνή, ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὰς ἐν τῷ πατρὶ προεννοηθείσας ἰδέας, ὅθεν κελεύοντος πατρὸς γίνεσθαι κόσμον τὸ κατὰ ἓν λόγος ἀπετελεῖτο ἀρέσκων θεῷ.
pass_a_gloss: This one therefore alone and according to all God first conceived in mind brings forth word, not word as sound, but inward thought of all reasoning. This one alone from existing things was generated; for the being itself was the Father, from whom the generated. The word was cause to the things being generated, carrying in itself the will of the generated one, not without the Father's thought; for at the same time as proceeding from the one generating, having become firstborn voice of this one, it has in itself the ideas preconceived in the Father, whence, the Father commanding to generate the world, the word according to one was being completed pleasing to God.

pass_b_english: God alone, according to all things, first conceives a thought and brings forth the Word, but not the Word as a spoken sound - rather, the inward thought that underlies all reasoning. This Word is the only one generated from existing things, because the Father Himself is the existing being from whom the generated Word comes. The Word is the cause of all things that come into being, and it carries within itself the will of the One who generated it, never straying from the Father's thought. As it proceeds from the Father, the Word becomes the firstborn Voice, containing within itself the ideas that the Father had already conceived. So when the Father commands the world to come into being, the Word brings it to completion in a way that pleases God.

review.notes: Pass B introduces a significant error in agency and meaning regarding the first sentence. The Greek 'Οὗτος οὖν μόνος καὶ κατὰ πάντων θεὸς λόγον πρῶτον ἐννοηθεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ' indicates that God (θεὸς) is the subject who conceives and brings forth the Word (λόγον). Pass B translates this as 'God alone, according to all things, first conceives a thought and brings forth the Word', which implies God conceives a thought *and then* brings forth the Word, whereas the Greek structure 'λόγον... ἐννοηθεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ' indicates that the Word is the object of the conception and the generation (the Word is the thing conceived and brought forth). Furthermore, Pass B's 'God alone... first conceives a thought' misrepresents 'μόνος' (alone), which in the Greek refers to the Word (Οὗτος... μόνος) being the only thing generated in this manner, not God being the only one who conceives.
reasons: Pass B misattributes the scope of 'μόνος' and the relationship between the conception and the Word. Greek: 'Οὗτος οὖν μόνος... λόγον... ἐννοηθεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ' (This one [the Word] alone... having been first conceived in mind, brings forth/is brought forth). Pass B: 'God alone... first conceives a thought and brings forth the Word'. This changes the subject/object relationship and the meaning of 'alone'.
